q: 'To be, or not to be: that is the question' - is from which drama?
explain: This is the opening line of Hamlet's famous soliloquy in Act 3, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's tragedy 'Hamlet'.

q: 'All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players' - is from?
explain: This famous line is spoken by Jaques in Act 2, Scene 7 of Shakespeare's comedy 'As You Like It'. It describes the seven ages of man.

q: 'O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo?' - Who says this?
explain: Juliet says this in Act 2, Scene 2 of 'Romeo and Juliet'. 'Wherefore' means 'why', not 'where'. She asks why he has to be Romeo, a Montague.

q: 'If music be the food of love, play on' - is the opening line of which play?
explain: This is the opening line spoken by Duke Orsino in Shakespeare's comedy 'Twelfth Night' (Act 1, Scene 1).

q: 'Fraility, thy name is woman!' - is a quote from -
explain: Hamlet says this in Act 1, Scene 2 after his mother's hasty marriage to Claudius. He expresses disgust at women's weakness.

q: 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever' - is from?
explain: This is the opening line of John Keats' poem 'Endymion' (1818). It is one of the most quoted lines in English poetry.

q: 'To err is human; to forgive, divine' - Who said this?
explain: This line is from Alexander Pope's poem 'An Essay on Criticism' (1711).

q: 'Child is the father of the Man' - is taken from?
options: Ode on Intimations of Immortality - Wordsworth
explain: This famous paradoxical line is from William Wordsworth's poem 'My Heart Leaps Up' (1802), which was later used as an epigraph for 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality' and also appears in 'The Rainbow'.

q: 'Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink' - is from?
options: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
explain: This line is from S.T. Coleridge's famous poem 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), a masterpiece of Romantic poetry.

q: 'Where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise' - Who wrote this?
explain: This line is from Thomas Gray's poem 'Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College' (1742).

q: 'We are such stuff As dreams are made on' - is from?
explain: Prospero says this in Act 4, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's last play 'The Tempest'. Full line: 'We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.'

q: 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?' - is from?
options: Ode to the West Wind - Shelley
explain: This optimistic closing line is from P.B. Shelley's poem 'Ode to the West Wind' (1819).

q: 'All that glitters is not gold' - is from?
explain: The original line 'All that glisters is not gold' is from Act 2, Scene 7 of 'The Merchant of Venice' spoken by the Prince of Morocco.

q: 'Truth is beauty, beauty truth' - is from?
options: Ode on a Grecian Urn - Keats
explain: Full line: 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know' from Keats' 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' (1819).

q: 'Brevity is the soul of wit' - Who said this?
explain: Polonius says this in Act 2, Scene 2 of 'Hamlet'. Ironically, Polonius himself is very long-winded.

q: 'Hell is empty and all the devils are here' - is from?
explain: Ariel says this in Act 1, Scene 2 of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest'.

q: 'Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven' - is from?
explain: This is spoken by Satan in Book 1 of John Milton's epic 'Paradise Lost' (1667).

q: 'Cowards die many times before their deaths; The valiant never taste of death but once' - is from?
explain: Caesar says this to Calpurnia in Act 2, Scene 2 of Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar'.

q: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' - is the opening line of?
explain: This is the opening line of William Wordsworth's most famous poem 'Daffodils' or 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' (1807).

q: 'O! What a noble mind is here o'erthrown' - Who says this?
explain: Ophelia says this in Act 3, Scene 1 of 'Hamlet' after seeing Hamlet's apparent madness.

q: 'Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em' - is from?
explain: Malvolio says this in Act 2, Scene 5 of Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night'.

q: 'The child is father of the man' and 'Nature never did betray the heart that loved her' - both are by?
explain: Both lines are by William Wordsworth. First from 'My Heart Leaps Up', second from 'Tintern Abbey'.

q: 'A little learning is a dangerous thing' - is from?
options: The Rape of the Lock - Pope
explain: This line is from Alexander Pope's 'An Essay on Criticism'. Full line: 'A little learning is a dangerous thing; Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring'.

q: 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships?' - is from?
explain: Dr. Faustus says this when he sees Helen of Troy in Christopher Marlowe's play 'Doctor Faustus' (Act 5, Scene 1).

q: 'Out, damned spot! out, I say!' - Who says this?
explain: Lady Macbeth says this in her sleepwalking scene (Act 5, Scene 1) of 'Macbeth', haunted by guilt after Duncan's murder.

q: 'Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player That struts and frets his hour upon the stage' - is from?
explain: Macbeth says this famous soliloquy in Act 5, Scene 5 after hearing of Lady Macbeth's death. It reflects the meaninglessness of life.

q: 'Blow, blow, thou winter wind, Thou art not so unkind As man's ingratitude' - is from?
explain: This song is sung by Amiens in Act 2, Scene 7 of 'As You Like It', comparing the harshness of winter wind with man's ingratitude.

q: 'O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn's being' - is from?
explain: Opening line of Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind' (1819).

q: 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee' - is from?
explain: This is the concluding couplet of Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'. It speaks about the immortality of poetry.

q: 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun' - is from?
explain: This is the opening line of Shakespeare's Sonnet 130, a satirical sonnet that mocks the exaggerated comparisons in love poetry.

q: 'The old order changeth, yielding place to new' - is from?
explain: This line is from Alfred Lord Tennyson's poem 'Morte d'Arthur' (1842).

q: 'Tis better to have loved and lost Than never to have loved at all' - is from?
explain: This famous line on love and loss is from Tennyson's 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' (1850), written after his friend Arthur Hallam's death.

q: 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield' - is from?
explain: This is the last line of Tennyson's dramatic monologue 'Ulysses' (1842), spoken by the Greek hero Ulysses.

q: 'I have promises to keep, And miles to go before I sleep' - is from?
options: Robert Frost - Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
Robert Frost - The Road Not Taken
explain: Closing lines of Robert Frost's famous poem 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' (1923).

q: 'Two roads diverged in a wood, and I— I took the one less traveled by' - is from?
explain: This is from Robert Frost's poem 'The Road Not Taken' (1916), often misinterpreted as a celebration of individuality.

q: 'Because I could not stop for Death – He kindly stopped for me' - is by?
explain: This is the opening line of Emily Dickinson's famous poem (c. 1863), personifying death as a kind carriage driver.

q: 'Do not go gentle into that good night, Old age should burn and rave at close of day' - is by?
explain: This villanelle is by Welsh poet Dylan Thomas (1951), written for his dying father. It urges resistance against death.

q: 'April is the cruellest month' - is the opening line of?
options: The Waste Land - T. S. Eliot
The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock - Eliot
explain: Opening line of T.S. Eliot's modernist masterpiece 'The Waste Land' (1922).

q: 'Let us go then, you and I' - is the opening line of?
options: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock - Eliot
Rhapsody on a Windy Night - Eliot
explain: Opening line of Eliot's 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' (1915).

q: 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold' - is from?
options: The Second Coming - W. B. Yeats
The Lake Isle of Innisfree - Yeats
explain: This line is from Yeats' famous poem 'The Second Coming' (1920), written after WWI. Chinua Achebe used it as his novel title.

q: 'O Captain! My Captain! our fearful trip is done' - is by?
explain: Walt Whitman wrote this elegy on Abraham Lincoln's death in 1865 after the American Civil War.

q: 'Hope is the thing with feathers That perches in the soul' - is by?
explain: This is one of Emily Dickinson's most famous poems (No. 254), using the metaphor of a bird for hope.

q: 'Good fences make good neighbours' - is from?
explain: This proverbial line is from Frost's poem 'Mending Wall' (1914).

q: 'A rose by any other name would smell as sweet' - is from?
explain: Juliet says this in Act 2, Scene 2 of 'Romeo and Juliet' – meaning names do not change the nature of things.

q: 'Et tu, Brute?' - is from?
explain: Julius Caesar says this in Act 3, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar' when he sees his friend Brutus among the assassins. Means 'You too, Brutus?'

q: 'The love that dare not speak its name' - is a line by?
explain: This line is from Lord Alfred Douglas' poem 'Two Loves' (1894). It was used against Oscar Wilde in his trial for homosexuality.

q: 'I am no orator, as Brutus is' - Who says this?
explain: Mark Antony says this in his famous funeral speech in Act 3, Scene 2 of 'Julius Caesar' – an example of irony.

q: 'The woods are lovely, dark and deep' - is from?
options: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening - Frost
explain: Line from Frost's 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening'.

q: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate' - is from?
explain: Opening line of Shakespeare's most famous Sonnet 18.

q: 'O Death, where is thy sting? O Grave, where is thy victory?' - is from?
explain: This is from John Donne's Holy Sonnet 10 'Death, be not proud'. The line is originally from Bible (1 Corinthians 15:55).

q: 'I have a dream' - famous speech by?
explain: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered this historic speech on 28 August 1963 at Lincoln Memorial during March on Washington for civil rights.

q: 'To err is human, to forgive is divine' is contrasted with 'To be or not to be' - which age do they belong to?
explain: Pope's 'To err is human' is Neoclassical (1711), Shakespeare's 'To be or not to be' is Elizabethan (1599-1601).

q: 'Knowledge is power' - Who said this?
explain: Francis Bacon wrote 'Knowledge is power' in his 'Meditationes Sacrae' (1597). Original Latin: 'Scientia potentia est'.

q: 'The unexamined life is not worth living' - is said by?
explain: Socrates said this at his trial, as quoted by Plato in Apology. It means life without self-reflection is meaningless.

q: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' - is the opening line of?
explain: Jean-Jacques Rousseau's 'The Social Contract' (1762) opens with this famous line about liberty and society.

q: 'I think, therefore I am' (Cogito, ergo sum) - Who said this?
explain: French philosopher Rene Descartes said this in 'Discourse on Method' (1637) as proof of existence.

q: 'Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they? Think not of them, thou hast thy music too' - is from?
options: Ode on a Grecian Urn - Keats
explain: From Keats' 'To Autumn' (1819), considered one of the most perfect short poems in English.

q: 'Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought' - Who said this?
explain: This line is from Shelley's 'To a Skylark' (1820) - comparing human songs with skylark's joyful song.

q: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud That floats on high o'er vales and hills' - next line is?
options: When all at once I saw a crowd
Beside the lake, beneath the trees
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze
explain: Second line of Wordsworth's 'Daffodils' (1807) is 'When all at once I saw a crowd'.

q: 'The best is yet to be, The last of life, for which the first was made' - is by?
explain: Robert Browning's 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' (1864) contains this optimistic line about old age.

q: 'Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind' - is from?
explain: Helena says this in Act 1, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.

q: 'We love to contemplate blue' - Wait, 'My soul is white, my heart is blue'? Who wrote 'She Walks in Beauty'?
explain: 'She walks in beauty, like the night' is Lord Byron's famous poem (1814) about his cousin Anne Wilmot.

q: 'O! She doth teach the torches to burn bright!' - Who says about whom?
explain: Romeo says this when he first sees Juliet in Act 1, Scene 5 of 'Romeo and Juliet'.

q: 'Let me not to the marriage of true minds Admit impediments' - is from?
explain: Opening line of Shakespeare's Sonnet 116, which defines true love.

q: 'If you have tears, prepare to shed them now' - is from?
explain: Mark Antony says this in Act 3, Scene 2 of 'Julius Caesar' before showing Caesar's wounded body.

q: 'The Child is father of the Man; And I could wish my days to be Bound each to each by natural piety' - Which poem?
explain: Full poem 'My Heart Leaps Up' (1802) by Wordsworth is: My heart leaps up when I behold A rainbow in the sky... The Child is father of the Man.

q: 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways' - Who wrote?
explain: Opening line of Sonnet 43 from 'Sonnets from the Portuguese' (1850) by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, written for her husband Robert Browning.

q: 'The only way to do great work is to love what you do' - is said by?
explain: Steve Jobs said this in his famous Stanford Commencement Speech in 2005.

q: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind' - Who said?
explain: Neil Armstrong said this on 20 July 1969 when he first stepped on the moon during Apollo 11 mission.

q: 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears' - is from?
explain: Mark Antony begins his funeral oration for Caesar with this line in Act 3, Scene 2 of 'Julius Caesar'.

q: 'To be a poet is to have a soul so quick to discern that no shade of quality escapes it' - Who said?
explain: Wordsworth defined poet in Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800) - 'Poet is a man speaking to men'.

q: 'O, beware, my lord, of jealousy! It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock The meat it feeds on' - Who says?
explain: Iago warns Othello about jealousy in Act 3, Scene 3 of 'Othello', though he himself plants jealousy in Othello's mind.

q: 'Had we but world enough and time, This coyness, lady, were no crime' - is from?
options: To His Coy Mistress - Andrew Marvell
To His Mistress Going to Bed - Donne
explain: Opening line of metaphysical poet Andrew Marvell's famous carpe diem poem 'To His Coy Mistress' (1681).

q: 'No man is an island, entire of itself' - Who wrote?
explain: From John Donne's 'Devotions upon Emergent Occasions' (1624), Meditation 17. Means all mankind is interconnected.

q: 'The road to hell is paved with good intentions' - is a proverb used by?
explain: Often attributed to Samuel Johnson, but similar line found in earlier works. Means good intentions without action lead to failure.

q: 'I have no spur To prick the sides of my intent, but only Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself' - Who says?
explain: Macbeth says this in Act 1, Scene 7 of 'Macbeth', contemplating murder of Duncan - his only motive is ambition.

q: 'A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!' - is from?
explain: King Richard III cries this in Act 5, Scene 4 of 'Richard III' when his horse is killed in battle of Bosworth Field.

q: 'I came, I saw, I conquered' (Veni, Vidi, Vici) - Who said?
explain: Julius Caesar reportedly said this in 47 BC after victory in Battle of Zela in Pontus.

q: 'The soul that can speak through the eyes can also kiss with a gaze' - is by?
explain: Spanish Romantic poet Gustavo Adolfo Becquer wrote this line.

q: 'If you cannot be a poet, be the poem' - Who said?
explain: American actor David Carradine popularized this line about living poetically.

q: 'O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright! It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope's ear' - This description is of?
explain: Romeo's first impression of Juliet at Capulet's feast in 'Romeo and Juliet' Act 1, Scene 5.

q: 'Death be not proud, though some have called thee Mighty and dreadful, for thou art not so' - is by?
explain: Opening line of Donne's Holy Sonnet 10, where poet challenges death's power.

q: 'But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun' - Who says?
explain: Romeo says this in the famous balcony scene, Act 2, Scene 2 of 'Romeo and Juliet'.

q: 'My name is Ozymandias, king of kings: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' - is from?
explain: From Shelley's sonnet 'Ozymandias' (1818) about impermanence of power and human pride.

q: 'The Waste Land' is dedicated to whom as 'il miglior fabbro' (the better craftsman)?
explain: T.S. Eliot dedicated 'The Waste Land' (1922) to Ezra Pound who heavily edited the poem. 'Il miglior fabbro' is from Dante.

q: 'A little knowledge is a dangerous thing' is often misquoted. The correct line is?
options: A little learning is a dangerous thing
explain: Correct is Pope's 'A little learning is a dangerous thing' from An Essay on Criticism. People often say knowledge instead of learning.

q: 'For oft, when on my couch I lie In vacant or in pensive mood' - next line is?
options: They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude
And then my heart with pleasure fills
explain: From Wordsworth's 'Daffodils' - 'They flash upon that inward eye Which is the bliss of solitude; And then my heart with pleasure fills, And dances with the daffodils.'

q: 'In three words I can sum up everything I've learned about life: it goes on' - is by?
explain: Robert Frost said this. It reflects his stoic philosophy of resilience.

q: 'To live is the rarest thing in the world. Most people exist, that is all' - Who said?
explain: From Oscar Wilde's 'The Soul of Man under Socialism' (1891).

q: 'The woods are lovely, dark and deep, But I have promises to keep' - What figure of speech is 'woods are lovely'?
options: Both imagery and metaphor for life's temptations
explain: Frost's woods symbolize temptation, death, and allure of rest. The line is rich in imagery.

q: 'I contain multitudes' - is from?
explain: Line from Whitman's 'Song of Myself' (1855) which is part of Leaves of Grass: 'Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)'

q: 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past' - last line of?
options: The Great Gatsby - F. Scott Fitzgerald
explain: Last line of Fitzgerald's 'The Great Gatsby' (1925), one of greatest closing lines in American literature.

q: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' - opening line of?
options: A Tale of Two Cities - Charles Dickens
explain: Opening of Dickens' 'A Tale of Two Cities' (1859) set during French Revolution: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times...'

q: 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others' - is from?
explain: From Orwell's satirical novella 'Animal Farm' (1945), mocking corruption of socialist ideals.

q: 'Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more' - Who says?
explain: Brutus says this in Act 3, Scene 2 of 'Julius Caesar' justifying his participation in assassination.

q: 'What's in a name? That which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet' - Who says to whom?
explain: Juliet says this to herself in balcony scene, Act 2, Scene 2 of Romeo and Juliet, lamenting Romeo's Montague name.

q: 'If music be the food of love, play on; Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, The appetite may sicken, and so die' - Spoken by?
explain: Duke Orsino, lovesick for Olivia, says this at very beginning of Twelfth Night.

q: 'I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul' - is from?
explain: Closing lines of Henley's 'Invictus' (1875), written from hospital bed. Nelson Mandela recited it in prison.

q: 'Do unto others as you would have them do unto you' - is known as?
explain: The Golden Rule, found in Bible (Matthew 7:12), also in many religions. Means treat others as you want to be treated.

q: 'The poet's eye, in a fine frenzy rolling, Doth glance from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven' - is from?
explain: Theseus speaks in Act 5, Scene 1 of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' about poet's imagination, lover and madman.
